meta.title: Who really said "When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Burke. The line sits on page 106 of his 1770 pamphlet Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents — unlike the "triumph of evil" line he never wrote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Burke, page 106 of his 1770 pamphlet. The famous "triumph of evil" version pinned to him is the fake — closest real antecedent is John Stuart Mill, 1867.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. Burke wrote it in Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents, the pamphlet he published on 23 April 1770 — the sentence appears on page 106 of the 1770 London printing for J. Dodsley, and again in his collected Works. It is not the same line as “the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing,” which Burke never wrote.

source.heading: The pamphlet it comes from

docMeta.dd: Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
23 April 1770 — London, printed for J. Dodsley, Pall Mall
Page 106 of the 1770 Dodsley printing (second edition); also in The Works of the Right Honourable Edmund Burke, Vol. I (Nimmo, 1887)

source.excerpt: No man, who is not inflamed by vainglory into enthusiasm, can flatter himself that his single, unsupported, desultory, unsystematic endeavors are of power to defeat the subtle designs and united cabals of ambitious citizens. When bad men combine, the good must associate; else they will fall, one by one, an unpitied sacrifice in a contemptible struggle.
trail: The scanned 1770 pamphlet — title page: “THE SECOND EDITION · LONDON, Printed for J. DODSLEY, in Pall-Mall · MDCCLXX” — carries the sentence on page 106 ↗, immediately after Burke’s argument that scattered, unconnected men cannot resist “united Cabals of ambitious citizens.”
The same passage appears in The Works of the Right Honourable Edmund Burke, Vol. I (London: John C. Nimmo, 1887), digitised by Project Gutenberg ↗, where the pamphlet begins at page 433.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section under Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770), citing Volume i, p. 526 — and puts “All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing” in a separate Misattributed section.
Quote Investigator ↗ quotes this Burke sentence from a 1770 Dodsley printing while concluding that the famous shorter saying cannot be found in Burke at all.
source.cutTag: Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770)
source.excerptNote: Punctuation drifts between printings: the collected Works text sets off the phrase with commas — “they will fall, one by one, an unpitied sacrifice” — while the version that circulates online, and the one Wikiquote prints ↗, drops them. The words themselves are identical.

author.name: Edmund Burke
author.heading: Who was Edmund Burke?
author.bio: Edmund Burke was an Anglo-Irish writer, philosopher and politician, born 12 January 1729 and died 9 July 1797, widely credited as the founder of the cultural and political philosophy of conservatism. He entered politics as private secretary to the Marquess of Rockingham in 1765 and spent his Commons career in the Rockinghamite Whig faction. Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770), where this line appears, was his major statement on constitutional limits to executive power — and a defence of party as an honourable thing.

misattribution.heading: The line people mean to quote — and the one Burke actually wrote
misattribution.intro: This sentence is genuine Burke. The trouble is that it is almost always dragged into an argument about a different sentence: the pithy “the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing,” which is the single most-quoted thing pinned on Burke and appears nowhere in his writings.

items.why: “All that is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing” sits in Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗, which notes that “an extraordinary number of variants of it exist, but all without any definite original source,” and lists dozens of circulating wordings.

In his inaugural address to the University of St Andrews, Mill wrote: “Bad men need nothing more to compass their ends, than that good men should look on and do nothing.” The line is on the page in the 1867 Longmans printing ↗ of the address.

items.scope: Earliest example of the credit to Burke
items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the earliest example it found of the saying being attributed to Burke is an address Hyslop delivered on 5 July 1920 — a century and a half after Burke’s pamphlet.
Some printings read “they will fall, one by one,” with commas — that is how the collected Works ↗ sets it — while the commonly shared form drops them. No words are added or changed.

misattribution.truthLine: Burke really did write “When bad men combine, the good must associate” — you can read it on page 106 of the 1770 pamphlet ↗. He did not write the snappier “triumph of evil” version that gets quoted in its place.

context.heading: Why Burke wrote it
lead: Burke published the pamphlet in April 1770 as a defence of organised political party at a moment when “party” was a dirty word. His target was what Wikipedia describes ↗ as the “king’s friends” and their “Double Cabinet” — a court faction he believed was working around the Commons to serve George III.

The sentence is the hinge of that argument. Burke had just insisted that a man acting alone, however virtuous, cannot defeat “the subtle designs and united cabals of ambitious citizens.” Honest men must therefore organise — which is exactly what a political party is for.
detailsBody: The pamphlet also contains Burke’s definition of party, which Wikipedia quotes ↗ alongside this very sentence: bodies “of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed.”

It is easy to see how a reader in a hurry could compress Burke’s point into “good men doing nothing lets evil win.” That compression is a fair summary of the idea — it is just not a quotation, and Burke is not the one who wrote it.
